title: Seller's Property Disclosure Statement
description: The District of Columbia Residential Real Property Seller Disclosure Act (D.C. Code § 42-1301 et seq.) requires sellers of residential real property containing 1 to 4 dwelling units to deliver a written disclosure statement, on the form approved by the Mayor (administered by DLCP, formerly DCRA), signed by the seller, before or at the time the purchaser executes the purchase agreement (D.C. Code § 42-1302). The Act applies only where the purchaser expresses in writing an intent to reside in the property. Exempt transfers include transfers between co-tenants, foreclosure sales, court-ordered transfers (probate, bankruptcy, divorce), and never-inhabited new construction (D.C. Code § 42-1301(b)).

required_actions.note: Deliver before or at the time the purchaser executes the purchase agreement. Applies only when the purchaser states in writing an intent to occupy the property as a residence.

metadata.note: Form approved by the Mayor; DC is a statutory-disclosure jurisdiction for 1-4 unit residential, not caveat emptor.

title: Brokerage Relationship Disclosure
description: D.C. Code § 42-1703 requires a licensee, upon having a substantive discussion about a specific property with an actual or prospective buyer or seller who is not the licensee's client, to disclose in writing any brokerage relationship the licensee has with another party to the transaction. Disclosure must be made at the earliest practical time and no later than when specific real estate assistance is first provided, and must be conspicuous (bold, all capitals, underlined, or in a separate box) if combined with other documents. Dual representation is permitted only with the written consent of all clients, and disclosure records must be retained for 3 years.

required_actions.note: Disclose at earliest practical time, no later than first specific real estate assistance. Dual representation requires written consent of all clients (D.C. Code § 42-1703).

title: Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (TOPA) Offer of Sale
description: Under the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (D.C. Code § 42-3404.02 et seq., part of the Rental Housing Conversion and Sale Act of 1980), before selling a tenant-occupied housing accommodation the owner must give each tenant (and the Mayor/DHCD) a written offer of sale and a bona fide opportunity to purchase, with tiered negotiation and settlement timelines based on building size. The TOPA Single-Family Home Exemption Amendment Act of 2018 (D.C. Law 22-120, effective July 3, 2018) exempts single-family accommodations, EXCEPT where a tenant who is elderly (62+) or has a disability signed a rental agreement by March 31, 2018 and took occupancy by April 15, 2018 — such tenants retain modified TOPA rights. An owner may deliver a written notice of intent to sell to determine elderly/disability status; the tenant has 20 days to respond. Sales made without required TOPA compliance are voidable.

required_actions.note: Deliver DHCD-prescribed Offer of Sale form to each tenant and file with the Mayor (DHCD) before contracting to sell. Negotiation/settlement periods scale with unit count (single-family exception cases, 2-4 units, 5+ units).
For single-family accommodations, verify whether any tenant qualifies under the elderly/disability exception of D.C. Law 22-120 before treating the sale as TOPA-exempt.

metadata.note: The District also holds its own purchase rights for larger buildings under DOPA, D.C. Code § 42-3404.31 et seq. (5+ unit accommodations).

title: Condominium Resale Certificate and Documents
description: D.C. Code § 42-1904.11 requires a unit owner reselling a condominium unit (other than the declarant) to obtain from the unit owners' association and furnish to the purchaser, on or before the 10th business day following contract execution, a copy of the condominium instruments and a resale certificate covering unpaid assessments (per D.C. Code § 42-1903.13(h)), capital expenditure plans, reserve funds, the most recent financial statement and operating budget, pending litigation, and insurance coverage. The purchaser may cancel the contract within 3 business days after receipt of the instruments and certificate and recover all deposits without deduction.

required_actions.document: Condominium instruments and resale certificate from the unit owners' association

required_actions.note: Purchaser has a 3-business-day right of rescission after receipt. Association must furnish the certificate within 10 days of a written request.

title: DC Lead-Hazard Disclosure (Pre-1978 Property)
description: In addition to the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule (42 U.S.C. § 4852d) for pre-1978 housing, the DC Lead-Hazard Prevention and Elimination Act (D.C. Code § 8-231.01 et seq.) imposes District-specific duties: paint on a pre-1978 dwelling is presumed to be lead-based, lead-based paint hazards are prohibited, and under D.C. Code § 8-231.04 the owner must provide required lead disclosures (including any available reports and pending DOEE actions) before the purchaser is obligated under any contract to purchase the dwelling unit. Use the DOEE lead disclosure form alongside the federal disclosure and EPA pamphlet.

required_actions.document: EPA 'Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home'

required_actions.note: Federal rule (FEDERAL-LEAD-PAINT-001) also applies: lead warning statement in contract and 10-day buyer inspection opportunity. DC presumes pre-1978 paint is lead-based unless tested otherwise.

metadata.note: DOEE administers the DC lead program; federal baseline is covered by FEDERAL-LEAD-PAINT-001.

title: DC Deed Transfer Tax and Recordation Tax
description: The District imposes a deed transfer tax on the transferor under D.C. Code § 47-903 and a deed recordation tax under D.C. Code § 42-1103, each at 1.1% of consideration for residential property under $400,000 and 1.45% (1.1% plus the 0.35% additional tax in effect since October 1, 2006) on the entire consideration for residential property of $400,000 or more — a combined 2.2% to 2.9%. The parties are jointly and severally liable by statute, but by custom the seller pays the transfer tax and the buyer pays the recordation tax. Form FP-7/C (Real Property Recordation and Transfer Tax return) must accompany the deed at recordation with the Recorder of Deeds.

required_actions.note: File the FP-7/C return and remit transfer and recordation taxes at recordation.

1.1% transfer + 1.1% recordation under $400,000; 1.45% each at $400,000 or more. Customary split: seller pays transfer tax, buyer pays recordation tax (negotiable; parties jointly and severally liable).

metadata.note: Qualifying first-time DC homebuyers may claim a reduced 0.725% recordation rate (income and purchase-price caps apply). Higher rates have applied to commercial/mixed-use deeds over $2M since 2019.

title: Title Company / Settlement Attorney Closing Jurisdiction
description: District of Columbia closings are customarily conducted by title companies or settlement attorneys rather than by escrow as on the West Coast; attorney presence is not statutorily mandated for the parties. Title insurance producers and settlement agents handling DC transactions must be licensed under the District of Columbia Title Insurance Producers Act of 2010 (D.C. Code § 31-5041.01 et seq.), which also governs handling of escrow and settlement funds. The buyer customarily selects the settlement provider, and under RESPA § 9 (12 U.S.C. § 2608) the seller may not condition the sale on the buyer purchasing title insurance from a particular company.

required_actions.note: Use a title insurance producer licensed under D.C. Code § 31-5041.01 et seq.; buyer customarily chooses the settlement provider.
